name: Esther Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year associate in the employment team at a mid-size firm, and most of our clients are workers, not companies. So a normal day is unfair dismissal claims, discrimination claims, a lot of reading emails people sent their managers at two in the morning. I get in at half eight, check the tribunal deadlines (a tribunal is the court that hears work disputes), then spend most of the day drafting witness statements and bundles, which are the big indexed folders of documents. The part I love is the first phone call with a client, when they finally tell someone what happened.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The billing target, honestly. I have to record six and a half hours of chargeable time a day, and a lot of our clients are on fixed fees or union funding, so every hour is watched. My supervisor, Priya, sends my drafts back covered in red, and she's usually right, which is worse. I go home to Jonas, my partner, who's a nurse on nights, and some weeks we only see each other on the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a tool that helps with the boring parts, like summarising a 400-page bundle, but it can't sit with a crying client. I'd probably post something about how the hype was used to scare workers into accepting worse deals. That's the line I'd take with friends too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not completely, because the pressure on me was never mainly about AI. My appraisal in March worries me more than any robot. I'm still the junior whose drafts come back covered in red. That appraisal decides whether I get the pay step. If the firm uses the tool to cut the hours it can bill for bundles, my chargeable time drops, and that looks bad on my numbers even if it isn't my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the research tool the firm approved, maybe twice a week, the way I do now, but only once Priya says it's fine for a task. I'd ask her for one statement a month that I draft start to finish, so my writing actually gets better. And I'd keep putting £250 a month into savings, because we've got about four months' cushion and our rent goes up in August.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with a small knot in my stomach. The knot is about me being good enough, not about machines. It's an odd comfort to know my worries would be ordinary ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rent going up in August. What happens if your appraisal doesn't go well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't get the step, which is about £2,000 a year, and the rent rise eats what I was saving. Jonas does extra shifts when we're short, and I hate that, because he already looks grey on his days off. I'd probably start looking at the union-side legal teams, where the pay is lower but the targets are kinder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our paralegal, Tunde, who does most of the bundling. If even plain AI cuts bundling time, his hours are the first thing a partner looks at. I'd tell him to ask for the tribunal-listing work too, so he's not just the person who staples things.

say: AI is a **useful tool** for summaries, but it can't sit with a **crying client**.
The hype was used to **scare workers** into accepting worse deals.
Employment law still needs **people** who listen.
think: I'm **relieved**, but my real pressure is my **appraisal in March**, not AI.
If bundles take fewer hours, my **chargeable time** drops and that looks bad on paper.
do: Keep using the **approved research tool** about twice a week, once my supervisor signs off on the task.
Ask for **one full statement** a month to draft myself, so my writing improves.
Save **£250 a month** before the August rent rise.
feel: **Steady**, with a small knot about being **good enough** at the job.
S0.quote: My appraisal in March worries me more than any robot. I'm still the junior whose drafts come back covered in red.
fieldNote: Her worry in a no-change world is about **skill and appraisal**, not technology, and she knows it.
She worries first for the **paralegal** whose bundling hours are easy to cut.
Money is tight but managed: four months saved, a **rent rise**, and a partner who picks up **extra shifts**.

steps.text: Draft one full witness statement a month and get it marked
Put £250 a month into savings before the August rent rise
Use the firm's approved research tool twice a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper policy before anyone feeds client files into these systems, because our clients are people whose jobs are already on the line. Online, I'd share things from employment lawyers pushing for rules on how firms use AI to cut staff. I'd say it calmly, because I think the argument is strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my exact job is the one that shrinks. Drafting, checking, building bundles, answering client emails: that's most of my day, and it's top of the list on that card. The firm would keep the partners and maybe fewer juniors, and I'm not the strongest junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the firm's AI training as soon as it's offered, even though I'm not a natural at this stuff, because I'd rather learn it on a Tuesday than be the one who never did. I'd join the lawyers' union branch that a friend from law school keeps telling me about, and push for a say in how the tools are brought in. And I'd move the savings target from four months up to six by next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way where I still have my hands on the wheel. There's time on that card, and I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for rules, but you'd also learn the tools. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I can want a speed limit and still learn to drive. If I refuse to learn AI, I'm just the first junior cut. Then I've got no voice in the meeting at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonas the night the firm announces it's bringing in the new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm not panicking yet and that I've already signed up for the training. Then I'd probably ask how the AI scheduling at his hospital is going, because nurses got the rota software first. Jonas would tell me the bit nobody plans for is who checks the machine when it gets it wrong, and maybe that's a job too.

say: We need a **firm policy** before client files go into AI systems.
Lawyers should push for **rules** on how firms use AI to **cut staff**.
think: Drafting, checking and bundles are **most of my day**, and they shrink first.
The firm keeps **fewer juniors**, and I'm not the **strongest junior**.
do: Sign up for the firm's **AI training** the first week it's offered.
Join the **lawyers' union branch** and push for a say on new tools.
Raise savings from **four to six months** by next summer.
feel: **Anxious**, but still with some **control** because there's time to adjust.
S1.quote: I can want a speed limit and still learn to drive. If I refuse to learn AI, I'm just the first junior cut.
fieldNote: She sees **regulation and learning** the tools as one strategy, not a contradiction.
She is honest that she's **not the strongest** junior, which sharpens the risk.
Her partner's hospital rota software gives her a **preview** of what's coming.

steps.text: Join the firm's AI training course in its first week
Join the lawyers' union branch a law-school friend recommends
Build savings from four to six months of costs by next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political choice, not weather. Governments can slow it, tax it and protect people, and I'd say that loudly, at work and online. I'd probably be at the first protest outside parliament with a homemade sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be out of a job by 2029, maybe sooner. Almost everything I do is thinking work at a desk, so I don't get the extra three years that the robots take. The only part that feels human is the first phone call with a client, and I'm not sure a firm would pay a junior just for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Jonas and cut what we can: the car goes, the holiday goes. I'd look hard at moving into a union's legal team or a law centre, because those places might keep people for the human part longer. And I'd join whatever campaign was fighting for income support, because I'd need it, and so would half my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry, which is easier to hold than frightened. I picture Priya's office empty, and that makes me feel sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before the robots mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's simple. My partner Jonas is probably fine for a while, because you can't automate turning a patient at 4am with software. So we'd live on his wage, which is roughly what mine is, and we'd stop saving for a flat. It's strange to think the person who didn't go to law school is the safe one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if you lose your income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car first, that's £300 a month with insurance. Then the gym, the streaming, the meals out with my law-school group. The last thing I'd cut is the money I send my mum, because she's on her own.

say: AGI's arrival is a **political choice**, and governments can slow and tax it.
I'd be at the first **protest outside parliament**.
think: I'd likely be out of a job by **2029**, because my work is all **desk work**.
Only the **first client call** feels human, and firms may not pay a junior for it.
do: Sell the **car** and cancel the holiday in the **first month**.
Apply to **union legal teams** and law centres that may keep people longer.
Join the campaign for **income support** for displaced workers.
feel: **Frightened** and angry, with the anger easier to carry than the fear.
S2.quote: My partner Jonas is probably fine for a while, because you can't automate turning a patient at 4am with software.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** within two years and plans to live on her partner's wage.
She notices the **irony**: the nurse is safer than the lawyer.
Anger works as a **coping tool** for her; it turns fear into campaigning.

steps.text: Sell the car and save £300 a month
Apply to union legal teams and community law centres
Vote and campaign for income support for displaced workers
Join the first protests outside parliament on AI job losses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before: this needs rules, and five years is enough time to make them if governments stop pretending. I'd say the profession should be bargaining now, not in 2030. I'd write to my MP, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a strange amount of time. I'd be 32, which is when I'd expect to be getting good at this, and that's exactly when it goes. I think I'd lose the job, just with more warning to cushion the fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to get really good at the human side: client care, tribunal hearings, settlement calls. I'd take the firm's AI courses so I can supervise the tools rather than compete with them. And I'd talk to Jonas about whether we hold off buying a flat, because a mortgage on one income in 2031 sounds terrifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I can actually picture. The worst part is the waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off buying a flat. Are there other plans that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids, maybe. We'd talked about trying in three years. I don't want to be home with a baby the same year my job disappears, and I hate that a computer gets a vote in that. So we might wait to see how it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it goes the way you fear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the engineers, really, more the people who decided profit came first and the governments that let them. I'd also blame my own profession a bit, because senior lawyers mostly cared whether their own pension pot was safe. Priya would say that's unfair, and maybe it is.

say: Five years is **enough time** to make rules if governments act.
The profession should be **bargaining now**, not in 2030.
think: At **32** I'd just be getting good, and that's when the job goes.
I'd still **lose the job**, only with more warning.
do: Spend two years building **hearing and client skills** that are hardest to replace.
Take the firm's courses so I can **supervise AI tools**.
Delay buying a **flat** until the picture is clearer.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan, but the **waiting** wears on me.
S3.quote: I don't want to be home with a baby the same year my job disappears, and I hate that a computer gets a vote in that.
fieldNote: Five years lands right at her **career peak**, which she finds cruel.
AI is reaching into **family plans**: the flat and children both wait.
She blames **profit-first decisions** and her own senior profession, not engineers.

steps.text: Take the firm's AI courses to supervise the tools
Hold off buying a flat and trying for children
Write to her MP asking for rules on AI job cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disaster if we waste it. At work I'd push for the firm to retrain juniors rather than just stop hiring them. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think ten years means I might be fine for most of my thirties and then not. I'd have time to move into something like mediation or a law centre, where the client is in the room. I'm not sure that work survives either, but it buys more time than drafting does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time mediation course in the next year or two, paid in instalments, around £1,500. I'd keep saving steadily, so we've got six months by the time I'm 30. And I'd stay in the union and push for a training fund for juniors, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. There's enough time that it feels like weather I can dress for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know when to make the jump to mediation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the firm stops hiring trainees, that's my sign. If there's no new intake for two years, the career ladder's gone. I'd rather be off it before it falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a law student today, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a law student to learn how to sit with people in trouble, because that's the last bit to go. And I'd say get a second skill, something with your hands or with groups, so you're not betting everything on one ladder.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if we use it and a disaster if we waste it.
Firms should **retrain juniors**, not just stop hiring them.
think: I might be fine for **most of my thirties**, then not.
**Mediation** keeps the client in the room and buys more time than drafting.
do: Start a **part-time mediation course** within two years, around **£1,500**.
Reach **six months of savings** by age 30.
Push the union for a **training fund** for juniors.
feel: **Uneasy** more than scared, because there's time to **prepare**.
S4.quote: When the firm stops hiring trainees, that's my sign. If there's no new intake for two years, the career ladder's gone.
fieldNote: She has a clear **trigger**: no trainee intake for two years means leave.
Her move is **sideways into mediation**, keeping the human contact she values.
With ten years her job looks safe **for now**, so worry turns into planning.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time mediation course costing about £1,500
Reach six months of savings by age 30
Push the union for a training fund for junior lawyers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time and Jonas would be carrying us both. What would help is income support that's actually decent, and retraining paid for by the companies making the money. Even a guarantee of six months' pay for anyone pushed out would change how I'd sleep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my mum. She's on her own and I send her £100 a month, and whatever happens to me happens to her too. People talk about young lawyers like we're all rich, but most of us are a few bad months from moving back home.

headlineQuote: People talk about young lawyers like we're all rich, but most of us are a few bad months from moving back home.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old** employment associate who mostly acts for **workers**, and loves the first client call.
She's honest that she's **still learning** and that her supervisor's red pen worries her more than any machine.
She learns AI tools once they're **approved**, and pairs that with **union action** and calls for rules.
Her plans shift from **saving** to **mediation** and law centres as the AGI date comes closer.
At home, her partner's **nurse wage** looks safer than her own, and she supports her **mum**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose her job fast and her **partner** would carry them both.
whatWouldHelp: Decent **income support** and **retraining** paid for by the companies profiting from AI.
A guarantee of **six months' pay** for anyone pushed out of work.
